objectives: Name a major key with six sharps or six flats
F# major has six sharps; Gb major has six flats
F# and Gb are the same sounding key written two ways, so the signature is what tells them apart

concept.title: The end of the road
concept.body: Grade 4 took the signatures as far as five. One more each way finishes the set this syllabus asks for. F# major has six sharps, adding E# after F# C# G# D# A#. Gb major has six flats, adding Cb after Bb Eb Ab Db Gb. Both look odd at first: E# is played where F sits, and Cb where B sits, but the letter has to be right or the scale would use one letter twice. Count the signature exactly as before — six sharps is F# major, six flats is Gb major.

teach.smartTip: Six sharps is F# major; six flats is Gb major. Count them — nothing else in the course has six.
teach.didYouKnow: Play F# major and Gb major on a piano and you press the same keys. They are *enharmonic*: the same sounds spelled differently. Composers choose whichever spelling makes the page easier to read.

objectives: Name the relative minor of a six-sharp or six-flat major key
D# minor shares F# major's six sharps; Eb minor shares Gb major's six flats
The relative-minor rule has not changed — count down a minor 3rd from the major tonic

concept.title: Two more relatives
concept.body: A minor key borrows its signature from the major key a minor 3rd above it. That rule has held since Grade 2 and it still holds here. Down a minor 3rd from F# is D#, so D# minor carries the same six sharps. Down a minor 3rd from Gb is Eb, so Eb minor carries the same six flats. These two are enharmonic with each other, exactly as their relative majors are. With them the course now covers every major and minor key up to six sharps and six flats.

teach.smartTip: Down a minor 3rd from the major tonic: F# major to D# minor, Gb major to Eb minor. Same signature, different home note.
teach.didYouKnow: Eb minor is the key of the 'Adagio for Strings' theme Barber later reworked, and of Shostakovich's most famous fugue subject. Six flats sound forbidding on paper and sit very comfortably under the hand.

lessons.title: Harmonic and melodic minor at six accidentals

objectives: Build the harmonic and melodic minor scales of D# minor and Eb minor
The raised 7th of D# harmonic minor is C double sharp, not D
A scale uses each letter once, which is what forces the double sharp

concept.title: When a sharp is not enough
concept.body: Harmonic minor raises the 7th degree by a semitone. In D# minor the 7th is C#, and raising it gives C *double sharp* — written with an x. It sounds like D, but calling it D would use the letter D twice and skip C, and a scale must step through all seven letters in order. The same rule gives Eb melodic minor its C natural and D natural going up. Work the letters out first, then decide what accidental each one needs. The pattern is the one you already know; only the spelling looks unfamiliar.

teach.smartTip: Write the seven letters first, in order, then add accidentals. That is what stops you writing D instead of Cx.
teach.didYouKnow: A double sharp exists because notation tracks **letters**, not sounds. Cx and D sound identical on a keyboard, but a violinist reading Cx in D# minor plays it as a leading note straining up to D# — a slightly different pitch, and a very different intention.

objectives: Name an interval wider than an octave
A compound interval keeps the quality of its simple form and adds 7 to the number
A major 3rd plus an octave is a major 10th, also called a compound major 3rd

concept.title: Adding the octave
concept.body: Every interval so far has fitted inside an octave. Wider ones are called *compound*. Work one out in two steps. First ignore the extra octave and name the interval as if the upper note were brought down: C up to E is a major 3rd. Then put the octave back by adding 7 to the number, keeping the quality unchanged: a major 3rd becomes a *major 10th*. The quality never changes, because moving a note by a whole octave does not alter how it sounds against the other note. Both names are correct — major 10th and compound major 3rd — and a Grade 5 paper prints the number form.

teach.smartTip: Name it as if it fitted in an octave, then add 7 to the number. Quality stays; only the number grows.
teach.didYouKnow: Compound intervals are how chord symbols get their names. The 9th, 11th and 13th in a jazz chord are a 2nd, a 4th and a 6th moved up an octave — stacked above the 7th so they colour the chord rather than crowd it.

lessons.title: Chord inversions: a, b and c

objectives: A triad can be arranged with any of its three notes in the bass — this is its position, or inversion
Root position (a) has the root in the bass; 1st inversion (b) has the 3rd in the bass; 2nd inversion (c) has the 5th in the bass
Name a chord in two steps: work out the triad (I, II, IV or V) by finding its root, then read the bass note to name the position — so a IV chord with its 3rd in the bass is IVb

concept.title: Chord inversions: a, b and c
concept.body: The same triad can be built up from any of its three notes. When the root is the lowest note the chord is in *root position* (a). When the 3rd is the lowest note it is in *1st inversion* (b). When the 5th is the lowest note it is in *2nd inversion* (c). The notes are the same — only which one sits at the bottom changes. To name an inverted chord, first find the root by stacking the notes in 3rds, name the triad from the key (I, II, IV or V — remember II is minor in a major key), then look at the lowest note to name the position. A IV chord with its 3rd in the bass reads as IVb.

teach.smartTip: The lowest note names the position, not the numeral. Find the root by stacking the notes in 3rds first, then check which member is in the bass: root = a, 3rd = b, 5th = c.
teach.didYouKnow: The little letters a, b and c are the ABRSM way of writing inversions. Elsewhere you may meet figured bass instead — IVb is the same chord a musician of Bach's day would have marked with a small 6 under the bass note.

objectives: Name the perfect, plagal and imperfect cadences from the two chords that make them
A cadence is named by where it **ends** and by what comes before it
Choose a suitable chord at a cadential point in C, G, D or F major

concept.title: How a phrase closes
concept.body: A cadence is the pair of chords that closes a musical phrase, like punctuation. Three are needed at this grade. A *perfect* cadence is V to I: the dominant falls home to the tonic and the phrase sounds finished, a full stop. A *plagal* cadence is IV to I: it also lands on the tonic but arrives from below, the 'Amen' at the end of a hymn. An *imperfect* cadence ends on V instead, so it does not resolve — a comma, not a full stop. Notice that perfect and plagal both **end** on the tonic. What separates them is the chord before it, so always work out both chords, never just the last.

teach.smartTip: Ends on V? Imperfect. Ends on I? Then look at the chord before: V makes it perfect, IV makes it plagal.
teach.didYouKnow: The plagal cadence is called the 'Amen cadence' because it is what generations of hymn books put under that word. Its softer arrival is why it feels like a benediction rather than a conclusion.

objectives: Recognise the German words for tempo that Grade 5 adds
German terms do the same job as the Italian ones you already know
Breit and bewegt describe the motion, not only the speed

concept.title: The other language on the page
concept.body: Grade 5 is where a second language arrives. Italian became the international language of musical instruction, but German composers often wrote in German, so a score by Schumann, Brahms or Mahler gives its directions in German. The tempo words map onto the Italian you already know: *langsam* is slow, like adagio; *schnell* is fast, like allegro; *mässig* is at a moderate speed, like moderato. *Lebhaft* means lively. Two of them describe how the music moves rather than how fast it goes: *bewegt* is with movement, and *breit* is broad and expansive, which usually means slower and heavier. You are not expected to speak German. You are expected to recognise about twenty words when they appear.

teach.smartTip: German nouns take a capital letter, so a capitalised word in a tempo marking is usually German, not emphasis.
teach.didYouKnow: Beethoven marked his late piano sonatas in both languages at once, giving the Italian and then the German. He was arguing, in print, that a composer should be understood at home.

lessons.title: German words for mood and degree

objectives: Recognise the German words for mood the syllabus names
The small words — sehr, wenig, nicht, ohne — modify the word beside them
A German marking is often built from two or three of these together

concept.title: Small words, built up
concept.body: Half of the German vocabulary is moods: *mit Ausdruck* with expression, *ruhig* peaceful, *traurig* sad, *zart* tender, *voll* full. The other half is the words that join them up, and they matter more than they look. *Sehr* is very, *wenig* is little, *ein wenig* is a little, *etwas* is somewhat, *immer* is always, *aber* is but, *mit* is with, *ohne* is without and *nicht* is not. German builds its instructions by stacking these, so a marking is read as a phrase rather than as one word: nicht zu schnell is not too fast, sehr langsam is very slow, and immer leiser und leiser is always quieter and quieter. Learn the small words and the long markings decode themselves.

teach.smartTip: Read a German marking from the small words out. Nicht and ohne reverse the word they attach to.
teach.didYouKnow: Mahler wrote some of the longest performance directions ever printed, including one asking for a passage to sound 'like a sound of nature'. Every word of it is built from this vocabulary.

objectives: Read the two pedal instructions and know which pedal each names
Una corda and tre corde are the soft pedal down and released
M.D. and M.S. tell you which hand plays a note

concept.title: Which pedal, and which hand
concept.body: These are the instructions a piano score gives that no other instrument needs. Two of them are pedalling. *Ped* marks where the sustaining pedal — the right one — goes down, and its release sign marks where it comes up. *Una corda* means one string and asks for the left pedal, which shifts the action so the hammers strike fewer strings and the tone softens; *tre corde*, three strings, releases it again. The other two sort out the hands. *Mano destra* (M.D.) is the right hand and *mano sinistra* (M.S.) is the left, and they appear when a note is written on a staff that the other hand would normally play.

teach.smartTip: Una corda and tre corde are the **left** pedal. Ped and its release are the right one.
teach.didYouKnow: Una corda is literally true on a grand piano: the action shifts sideways so each hammer hits two of the three strings, or one on older instruments. On an upright the pedal moves the hammers closer instead, which is why the effect is weaker.

objectives: A transposing instrument sounds at a different pitch from the note it reads — a B♭ clarinet, A clarinet and horn in F all **sound lower** than they are written
To make the instrument sound at concert pitch, write its part **higher** than the concert note — up a major 2nd for a B♭ clarinet, a minor 3rd for an A clarinet, a perfect 5th for a horn in F
The written part takes the key signature of its transposed key, so the spelling comes from that key — not accidentals added against the concert key

concept.title: Transposing instruments
concept.body: Some instruments do not sound the note they read. A B♭ clarinet reads a written C but **sounds** the B♭ a tone (major 2nd) below it; an A clarinet sounds a minor 3rd below; a horn in F sounds a perfect 5th below. Because the instrument sounds **lower** than written, you must write its part **higher** than concert pitch by that same interval — so a concert-pitch line for a B♭ clarinet is written up a major 2nd. The written part sits in a new key, a major 2nd (or minor 3rd, or perfect 5th) higher than the concert key, and you notate it with **that** key's signature — the accidentals come from the key signature, not from marking each note. Concert C major written for a B♭ clarinet becomes D major.

teach.smartTip: Sounds lower → write higher. B♭ clarinet up a major 2nd, A clarinet up a minor 3rd, horn in F up a perfect 5th. Change the key signature to the transposed key and let it spell the notes.
teach.didYouKnow: Composers write for transposing instruments so a clarinettist can switch between the B♭ and A clarinet reading the **same** fingerings — the part is rewritten, but the hands do not have to relearn a thing.

objectives: An ornament sign is shorthand for a fixed pattern of notes — read the written-out pattern and you can name the sign that stands for it
A mordent is a single quick flick to a neighbour and back; a turn wraps above and below the note; a trill is a longer measured wobble with the note above
A grace note leaning into the main note is an acciaccatura (crushed, very short) or an appoggiatura (on the beat, taking half the note's value)

concept.title: From the notes to the sign
concept.body: Every ornament sign is just a shorthand for notes a composer could have written out in full. An *upper mordent* is the note, the note above, and back — a single quick flick; a *lower mordent* flicks to the note below instead. A *turn* winds around the note: up to the note above, back to the note, down to the note below, and back again. A *trill* is a longer, measured alternation between the note and the note above it. Grace notes lean into the main note: an *acciaccatura* is crushed in as fast as possible (written as a tiny slashed note), while an *appoggiatura* leans on the beat and takes half the main note's value. Read the written-out pattern, work out which of these it is, and pick its sign.

teach.smartTip: Count the notes and their shape. Three notes flicking to a neighbour = a mordent; five notes winding above **and** below = a turn; a long even wobble = a trill; one small note leaning in = a grace note (slashed = acciaccatura, half-value = appoggiatura).
teach.didYouKnow: Baroque composers often left ornaments as signs precisely because the exact notes were a matter of taste — the same trill sign could be played a dozen ways depending on the player and the tempo.

objectives: Read notes in the tenor clef
The tenor clef is a C clef whose middle C sits on the 4th line
It is the alto clef moved up one line, so every note reads a 3rd lower

concept.title: The C clef moves up a line
concept.body: The tenor clef is the same C-clef symbol you met at Grade 4, printed one line higher. Its two curls point at the 4TH line, and that line is middle C. Everything follows from that. The bottom line is D3 and the top line is E4, so the whole stave sits lower than the alto clef reads. If you already know the alto clef, shift every note down a 3rd and you have the tenor. Find middle C on the 4th line first, every time, then count up or down from it. Cellists, bassoonists and trombonists all read this clef for their higher passages, which is exactly why it exists — it keeps those notes on the stave instead of stranding them on ledger lines.

teach.smartTip: Find the 4th line — that is middle C. Count from there, never from the bottom of the stave.
teach.didYouKnow: A cello part can switch bass, tenor and treble clef within a single phrase. The clef changes so the notes stay on the stave; the player is not changing instrument, only changing the ruler they are reading against.

objectives: Rewrite a melody at the octave from any clef into any other
The pitch letters never change — only the clef and the octave do
Work out the direction first: the new clef decides whether the notes go up or down

concept.title: The same tune, a different ruler
concept.body: You have transposed at the octave between treble and bass, and to and from the alto clef. With the tenor clef there are four clefs and any pair of them can be asked for. Nothing new happens. Write the same letter names in the new clef, an octave above or below, and keep every note value exactly as it was. The only judgement is direction, and the clefs decide it: bass reads lowest, then tenor, then alto, then treble. Moving to a higher-reading clef means writing the notes an octave up; moving to a lower one means an octave down. Work out the first note, check it against the key signature, then let the shape of the melody carry the rest.

teach.smartTip: Order the clefs by how high they read — bass, tenor, alto, treble. Moving up the list means writing up an octave.
teach.didYouKnow: This is exactly what a copyist did by hand before software. Getting the direction wrong put a cello line an octave under the double basses, which is the kind of mistake that is heard immediately and fixed in the first rehearsal.

lessons.title: Rewriting between simple and compound time

objectives: Simple and compound time have the same number of beats — 2/4 and 6/8 are both two-beat (duple) metres
To rewrite from simple into compound, each beat's note values grow by half: a crotchet beat becomes a dotted-crotchet beat, and every note inside gains a dot
To rewrite from compound back into simple, take the dot off every note — the values shrink by a third

concept.title: Same beats, re-valued notes
concept.body: Simple and compound time can describe the **same** number of beats — 2/4 and 6/8 are both duple. The difference is how the beat divides (in two for simple, in three for compound) and how the beat is written: a simple beat is a plain crotchet, a compound beat is a **dotted** crotchet. To rewrite a bar from simple into compound time you scale every note value by a half — add a dot to each note, so a crotchet becomes a dotted crotchet and a quaver becomes a dotted quaver. Going the other way, you take the dot off. The pitches never change — a metre rewrite re-values the rhythm, it does not re-pitch the melody. The note values you write in the two metres are **different**, even though the beats line up.

teach.smartTip: Same pitches, same order — just re-value. Into compound: add a dot to every note. Back to simple: take every dot off. The beats stay lined up.
teach.didYouKnow: 6/8 and 3/4 use the exact same six quavers per bar, but group them differently — 6/8 as two dotted-crotchet beats, 3/4 as three crotchet beats. The time signature tells the player how to **feel** the bar, not just how to count it.

objectives: Recognise 5/4, 7/4, 5/8 and 7/8 as irregular time signatures
Five and seven beats split into no equal groups, so the metre is neither simple nor compound
The beaming shows how the bar is grouped — usually 3+2 for five, 3+2+2 for seven

concept.title: When the beats do not divide evenly
concept.body: Every metre so far has split into two, three or four equal beats. Five and seven do not. A bar of 5/8 cannot be two equal halves or three equal thirds, so it is neither simple nor compound — it is *irregular*. What replaces the even split is a grouping, and the beaming on the page is what shows it. Five is usually written 3+2, and seven as 3+2+2, though a composer may choose 2+3 or another order and beam it that way. So read the beams first: they tell you how the bar is meant to be felt, which no time signature on its own can.

teach.smartTip: Count the beats. Five or seven means irregular — then look at the beams to see how they group.
teach.didYouKnow: Irregular metres are the normal case in Balkan dance music, where a 7/8 grouped 2+2+3 has been danced for centuries. Western notation only needed a name for them once composers started borrowing them.

objectives: An irregular bar has no equal beats, so the beams define the groups
5/8 is normally grouped 3 + 2 and 7/8 as 3 + 2 + 2
Regrouping the same notes changes how the bar is felt

concept.title: The beams are the metre
concept.body: Five and seven do not divide into equal beats, so an irregular bar has to say how it is grouped, and the beams are how it says it. A bar of 5/8 is normally written as a group of three quavers followed by a group of two, and 7/8 as three then two then two. Other readings exist, and a composer who wants 2 + 3 writes the beams that way. That is the point: in irregular time the grouping is not implied by the time signature the way it is in 3/4, so nothing but the beaming tells a player where the accents fall.

teach.smartTip: Read the beams before you play. In an irregular metre they are the only thing that fixes the accents.
teach.didYouKnow: Bulgarian and Greek dance music is full of 7/8. Players name the groups aloud, calling them long-short-short rather than counting to seven.

objectives: Name a quintuplet, sextuplet and septuplet from the number in the bracket
Each squeezes that many equal notes into one beat
A beat that normally holds four semiquavers holds five, six or seven instead

concept.title: Squeezing extra notes into a beat
concept.body: A triplet puts three notes where two would go. The same trick works with any number. In simple time a crotchet beat normally holds four semiquavers; write five under a bracket marked 5 and you have a *quintuplet*, six a *sextuplet*, seven a *septuplet*. The bracket number says how many notes are squeezed in. It does not say what they replace — that is always one beat, whatever the number. So a quintuplet and a septuplet both last exactly one beat; the septuplet's notes are simply faster.

teach.smartTip: The bracket number is how many you play. What they replace is always one beat — here, four semiquavers.
teach.didYouKnow: Chopin wrote runs of eleven, thirteen and even thirty-five notes over a single beat. The bracket number stops being a rhythm to count and becomes an instruction to play the flourish in the time available.

objectives: Four-part (SATB) writing splits into Soprano, Alto, Tenor and Bass, braced together on a grand staff of treble and bass staves
The treble staff carries the two upper voices (Soprano stem up, Alto stem down); the bass staff carries the two lower voices (Tenor stem up, Bass stem down)
Stem direction tells you which voice you are reading even when two voices share a staff — up-stems are the higher voice of the pair, down-stems the lower

concept.title: Four voices, one grand staff
concept.body: Choral and keyboard writing in four parts is named for its voices from top to bottom: *Soprano*, *Alto*, *Tenor*, *Bass*. All four are braced together on a *grand staff* — the treble staff above, the bass staff below. Each staff carries two voices, told apart by stem direction: on the treble staff, Soprano's stems point **up** and Alto's point **down**; on the bass staff, Tenor's stems point **up** and Bass's point **down**. So the staff tells you treble pair or bass pair, and the stem tells you which of that pair — the higher voice always stems up, the lower voice always stems down. The lowest-**sounding** voice overall is always the Bass, on the bass staff with its stem pointing down.

teach.smartTip: Staff first, then stem: treble staff = Soprano or Alto, bass staff = Tenor or Bass. Stem up = the higher voice of that pair (Soprano, Tenor); stem down = the lower voice (Alto, Bass).
teach.didYouKnow: SATB writing comes from choral music, where the four voice types sit in that same top-to-bottom order — but the same layout works just as well for four-part keyboard harmony with no singers at all.

objectives: Six voice types: soprano, mezzo-soprano and contralto; tenor, baritone and bass
Every instrument sets something vibrating, and the family follows from what
A reed can be single or double, which separates clarinet from oboe

concept.title: What is actually vibrating
concept.body: Grade 5 asks two things about performers. The first is the voice types, three to a group and named from the top down: soprano, mezzo-soprano and contralto for the higher voices, tenor, baritone and bass for the lower ones. The second is how an instrument makes its sound, which is also what puts it in a family. A string is set going by a bow or a finger. A woodwind sounds either through a reed, single on the clarinet and double on the oboe and bassoon, or through air directed across an edge, as on the flute, which is why the flute has no reed at all. Brass sounds from the player's own lips buzzing into a mouthpiece. Percussion is struck, and on the timpani what vibrates is a stretched skin.

teach.smartTip: Ask what vibrates. The answer names the mechanism and the family in one go.
teach.didYouKnow: The flute counts as woodwind although modern ones are silver. Family is decided by how the sound is made, not by what the tube is made of.

objectives: Read a passage using the full Grade 5 range and vocabulary
Answer general questions about a piece, as the exam paper asks
Work from the page, not from memory of the rules

concept.title: The last question on the paper
concept.body: The general-observation question comes near the end of a Grade 5 paper and it draws on everything before it. The passage may sit in any key to six sharps or flats, in an irregular metre, on any of the four clefs, and it may carry German terms as readily as Italian ones. No single fact is beyond what you have already met. What is being tested is whether you can find the relevant one without being told which it is. Read in the fixed order, answer the question that was actually asked, and check the answer against the page rather than against what you remember the rule to be.

teach.smartTip: Clef, key signature, time signature, then notes. The same order every time.
teach.didYouKnow: Examiners write the general-observation question last, after the rest of the paper is set, so that it uses only what the paper has already asked about.
